parsed_output.paper_title: Some Methods for Classification and Analysis of Multivariate Observations
parsed_output.authors_year: J. MacQueen, 1967
parsed_output.research_question: How can an N-dimensional population be partitioned into k sets on the basis of a sample to achieve efficient within-class variance, and what is the asymptotic behavior of the k-means process?
parsed_output.context: The work stems from problems in optimal classification related to optimal information structures and economical data processing on digital computers for similarity grouping, nonlinear prediction, distribution approximation, and independence tests.
methods: Mathematical analysis using martingale theory and measure theory
Computer experiments on multivariate data samples (e.g., student environments, semantic differential measurements, documents, physiological observations)
main_findings: The k-means procedure converges almost surely under specific continuity and boundedness assumptions.
The k-means process can be adapted for similarity grouping, relevant classifications, distribution approximation, and a scrambled dimension test for independence.
assumptions: Probability measure p is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on EN.
p(R) = 1 for a closed and bounded convex set R in EN, with p(A) > 0 for every open set A in R.
limitations_explicit: The k-means procedure will not in general converge to an optimal partition, although there are special cases where it will.

potential_open_questions.question: Can the k-means process be modified or bounded to eliminate slow indefinite oscillations around the center in certain symmetric distributions?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: Theorem 1 establishes almost sure convergence but does not eliminate potential slow oscillations around the center.
potential_open_questions.evidence: The k-means thus converge to some such relative position, but theorem 1 does not quite permit us to eliminate the interesting possibility that the two means oscillate slowly but indefinitely around the center.

potential_open_questions.question: What is the exact statistical power of the proposed scrambled dimension test for independence across various high-dimensional settings?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: Lack of an available computer program to run large numbers of scrambled samples using punched cards during the study.
potential_open_questions.evidence: The power of this procedure remains to be seen. A computer program was not available to do the scrambling, and its being inconvenient to set up large numbers of scrambled samples using punched cards, further testing of this method was not undertaken.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: For fixed marginal distributions, the within-class variance for the optimal partition is maximal when the joint distribution is actually the product of the marginals.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Intuition and inspection of sample behavior suggest that scrambling to destroy relationships increases the within-class variance.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: On the encouraging side is the related conjecture, that for fixed marginal distributions, the within-class variance for the optimal partition as defined in section 1 is maximal when the joint distribution is actually the product of the marginals.

parsed_output.paper_title: TRIMMED k-MEANS: AN ATTEMPT TO ROBUSTIFY QUANTIZERS
parsed_output.authors_year: J. A. Cuesta-Albertos, A. Gordaliza and C. Matrán (1997)
parsed_output.research_question: How can k-means clustering be robustified against outliers using impartial trimming, and what are the existence, characterization, and strong consistency properties of such trimmed k-means?
parsed_output.context: Traditional k-means clustering and joint location M-estimators can be highly unstable and lack robustness in the presence of outliers or contamination. While trimming procedures are useful, standard techniques suffer from arbitrariness in selecting zones for data removal. Building on Gordaliza's impartial trimming concept, this paper extends trimming to robustify k-means and analyzes its theoretical consistency.
methods: Formulation of impartial trimming functions and trimmed k-variation using penalty functions
Mathematical proofs for the existence and characterization of trimmed k-means
Proof of strong consistency of empirical trimmed k-means using the Skorohod representation theorem and continuity results
Simulation studies on bivariate normal distributions with mixture contamination (outliers and inliers) to evaluate robustness and mean estimation bias
Simulated annealing-based random optimization algorithm implemented in Matlab to handle the nonexistence of deterministic optimal algorithms
main_findings: The optimal trimming function essentially coincides with the indicator function of a nonpathological set formed by the union of k balls of equal radius (Corollary 3.2)
Trimmed k-means induces a partition of the optimal ball into k clusters, and each cluster center is a penalty-mean of X given that cluster (Proposition 3.3)
Proof of existence of trimmed k-means under mild continuity and growth conditions on the penalty function (Theorem 3.1)
Proof of strong consistency of trimmed k-means and trimmed k-variation under continuity of the limit probability distribution (Theorem 3.6)

Simulations show the method successfully detects anomalies and estimates cluster means, though a bias appears at low trimming levels due to probability mass distribution on the boundary of trimming balls
assumptions: The penalty function Phi is continuous, nondecreasing, with Phi(0)=0 and Phi(x) < infinity for all x
The probability measure PX of the limit random vector is continuous
The number of clusters k and the trimming level alpha are given and fixed
limitations_explicit: There is no deterministic optimal algorithm to choose the optimal trimming set, requiring heuristic optimization such as simulated annealing (Sections 1 and 4)

The theoretical breakdown point depends heavily on the data and can be low if the underlying distribution contains dense mass concentrations or contamination proportional to cluster weights (Section 5)
All clusters obtained by the method are forced to be spherical and have the same radius (Corollary 3.2 and Section 4)

potential_open_questions.question: How can the breakdown point of alpha-trimmed k-means be explicitly bounded or improved when clusters have unequal proportions or complex shapes?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The breakdown point depends heavily on the data structure and underlying cluster probabilities rather than being universally robust across all configurations.
potential_open_questions.evidence: Section 5 discusses an example where the breakdown point of the alpha-trimmed k-means can be as close to 0 as desired depending on the configuration and data distribution.

potential_open_questions.question: What are the exact asymptotic convergence rates and limiting distributions for empirical trimmed k-means estimators?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: While strong consistency is established, deriving the exact limiting distribution is complicated by discontinuities of the trimming functions on the boundaries of the balls.
potential_open_questions.evidence: Section 3 mentions that trimming functions are discontinuous on the boundary of corresponding balls, requiring careful handling of convergences without providing a full central limit theorem for trimmed k-means.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: If the penalty function Phi is continuously differentiable and strictly convex, then there is no probability mass at the boundary between clusters.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Smoothness and strict convexity eliminate boundary ambiguity in cluster assignments and partition geometry.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: Section 3 cites previous work (Cuesta-Albertos, Gordaliza and Matrán, 1995) establishing this property under continuously differentiable, strictly convex penalty functions.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: For a probability Q supported by exactly k clusters with respective probabilities q_1, ..., q_k, the breakdown point of the alpha-trimmed k-mean is at most min(alpha, q_1, ..., q_k) independently of the penalty function.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Contamination exceeding the relative mass of individual natural clusters forces the estimator to capture anomalous points as valid clusters or trim valid data.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: Section 5 analyzes the behavior of trimmed k-means under contaminated discrete uniform setups and deduces bounds on the breakdown behavior relative to cluster probabilities.

parsed_output.paper_title: Trimming Tools in Exploratory Data Analysis
parsed_output.authors_year: Luis Angel García-Escudero, Alfonso Gordaliza & Carlos Matrán (2003)
parsed_output.research_question: How can trimmed k-means methodology be used to propose exploratory graphical techniques to distinguish between the bulk of data and outlying observations, discover the number of clusters, and handle different kinds of contamination?
parsed_output.context: Exploratory data analysis where cluster analysis and outlier detection are closely related, focusing on overcoming the lack of robustness in classical k-means and the difficulty of determining the number of clusters k.
methods: Trimmed k-means methodology and impartial trimming procedure
Empirical trimmed k-variance functionals plotted against trimming sizes
Numerical second derivatives of trimmed variance curves to identify peaks and rates of decrease
Modified FAST-MCD algorithm utilizing a K-mean-step for computational implementation
Generalization to mixtures of elliptical distributions using scatter estimation matrices
main_findings: Plotting trimmed k-variance against trimming size alpha yields curves whose rates of decrease and second derivative peaks provide guidance for choosing the correct number of clusters k and cluster sizes.
The method can differentiate between outlying groups (small clusters) and radial outliers (isolated points).
Case studies on Old Faithful Geyser, Swiss Bank Notes, and simulated data demonstrate successful identification of cluster structure and contamination.
Replacing spherical distance metrics with covariance-based criteria allows the detection of non-spherical (linear) clusters.
assumptions: Data can be modeled as mixtures of spherical distributions (initially) or mixtures of elliptical distributions (generalized case)
Distributions are continuous for functional continuity properties to hold
limitations_explicit: The basic procedure is specially aimed at mixtures of spherical distributions because optimal zones are unions of balls, which is a drawback for more general mixtures.
Trimmed k-means and the graphical methods have high computational complexity requiring combinatorial exploration of data subsets.

potential_open_questions.question: How can the methodology be fully generalized to handle arbitrary metrics or distances specially designed for complex non-spherical problem domains?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: Current generalizations focus primarily on elliptical scatter matrices, and alternative custom discrepancy measures between specialized points and datasets remain an active direction of ongoing work.
potential_open_questions.evidence: We believe that this methodology could be interesting, because it allows the consideration of metrics specially designed for each problem. We are currently working in this direction.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: Replacing the spherical trimmed k-variance functionals with criteria based on log-determinants of scatter estimation matrices will successfully recover structure in highly linear or non-spherical clusters.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Standard trimmed k-means fails on linear clusters because Euclidean distance assumes spherical variance; incorporating group-specific covariance matrices accounts for varying shapes.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: Curves W1 and W2 do not allow us to detect properly the two-clusters structure... However, in Figure 8 (bottom) we see a clear 'jump' at alpha = 0.5 when k = 1 in the curve obtained plotting the values obtained from (4.1) against alpha.

parsed_output.paper_title: Implementing the Fisher's Discriminant Ratio in a k-Means Clustering Algorithm for Feature Selection and Data Set Trimming
parsed_output.authors_year: Thy-Hou Lin, Huang-Te Li, and Keng-Chang Tsai, 2004
parsed_output.research_question: How can Fisher's discriminant ratio implemented within a k-means clustering algorithm perform simultaneous feature selection and data set trimming to improve statistical significance in 3D-QSAR studies?
parsed_output.context: The study evaluates 221 human immunodeficiency virus type-1 (HIV-1) protease inhibitors with 43 computed molecular descriptors to construct quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) and CoMFA models.
methods: Computing 43 molecular descriptors (topological, geometric, electronic, and 3D-QSAR)
Scaling descriptor values between 1 and 0
Dividing the 221 inhibitors into classes based on pKi values
Applying Fisher's discriminant ratio for feature selection considering cross-correlation
Using a k-means clustering algorithm to generate clusters within each class and identifying bad clusters with smaller descriptor values to trim outliers
Linear regression, MREG stepwise variable selection, Cerius2 PLS, and SYBYL CoMFA PLS regression analyses
main_findings: Dividing the dataset into five classes yields the best feature selection result.
Topological descriptors such as Hosoya Z4, Z6, and Z3 are among the most class-sensitive features.
Trimming outliers using k-means clustering based on three selected descriptors retains 98 inhibitors (44%) and improves q2 to 0.727.
Subsequent CoMFA and Cerius2 PLS regression analyses on the retained 98 inhibitors show substantially increased statistical significance.
assumptions: Descriptors should take distant values in different classes and closely located values in the same class.
Inhibitors present in all bad clusters across selected descriptors are outliers and should be discarded.
Class separability is the primary criterion to evaluate feature selection and data set trimming.
limitations_explicit: The k-means clustering algorithm and feature selection approach are not invariant under a transformation of the variables.

potential_open_questions.question: Can alternative classification techniques beyond k-means clustering provide more effective data set trimming without requiring a priori distribution knowledge?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: While k-means performs well, other classifiers might handle complex decision boundaries differently.

parsed_output.paper_title: Robust k-means: a Theoretical Revisit
parsed_output.authors_year: Alexandros Georgogiannis (2016)
parsed_output.research_question: What are the robustness and consistency properties of robust k-means (RKM) under arbitrary and well-structured datasets?
parsed_output.context: Clustering noisy data using robust variants of quadratic k-means, specifically focusing on regularization/penalized methods (robust k-means) and their relationship to trimmed k-means.
methods: Theoretical analysis using variational analysis and Moreau envelopes
Finite sample breakdown point analysis
Vapnik-Chervonenkis theory for consistency properties
Synthetic data experiments comparing RKM and trimmed k-means on Gaussian mixtures
main_findings: Two outliers are enough to break down the cluster centers in robust k-means under general conditions.
When datasets are well-structured (e.g., balanced with separated balls of inliers), robust k-means effectively ignores outliers.
The universal breakdown point of robust k-means with unbiased proximal maps is 2/n.
Non-asymptotic consistency results for standard quadratic k-means remain valid for the robust variant even when penalties are non-convex.
assumptions: Observations can be decomposed into an inlier part and an error/outlier term penalized by a group penalty.
Proximal maps are either biased (convex penalties) or unbiased (non-convex penalties like l0-norm).
Datasets in the restricted robustness analysis contain balanced clusters covered by balls of bounded radius that are sufficiently far apart.
limitations_explicit: Robust k-means cannot be robust against any arbitrary type of contamination and any type of dataset when general universal breakdown points are considered.

potential_open_questions.question: How can robust k-means formulations be extended to handle high-dimensional overlapping clusters effectively without strict separation assumptions?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: Current theoretical guarantees rely heavily on the assumption that inlier clusters are well-separated by a minimum distance v.
potential_open_questions.evidence: The analysis in Section 3.3 and Theorem 2 requires centers of the balls to be at least v apart.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: Adaptive choice of the regularization parameter lambda can improve outlier rejection rates in multi-scale cluster densities.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Fixed global thresholds like lambda may either under-penalize heavy contamination or over-penalize tight inlier groups in complex mixtures.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: Section 5 demonstrates that grid search for lambda is required to match performance under different contamination scenarios.

parsed_output.paper_title: K-means-sharp: modified centroid update for outlier-robust k-means clustering
parsed_output.authors_year: Peter O. Olukanmi and Bhekisipho Twala, 2017
parsed_output.research_question: How to preserve the structure, simplicity and efficiency of the classical k-means while addressing its non-robustness to outliers by modifying only the centroid update step?
parsed_output.context: Real-world datasets commonly contain noise and outliers. Classical k-means is a least-squares method that assumes the absence of outliers, making it extremely sensitive because outliers contribute false large values to the objective function and skew cluster regionalization.
methods: Modifying the centroid update step of classical k-means to exclude putative outliers from the mean computation
Automated outlier detection via a global point-to-centroid distance threshold T derived from the distribution of point-to-centroid distances
Using sigma = 1.4826 MAD_e as an unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation
Setting the distance threshold T to 3 sigma (or 4.4478 MAD_e)
Evaluating performance using 10 datasets (2 standard datasets: Iris and Ruspini, and 4 outlier-contaminated versions of each with 5%, 10%, 15%, and 20% gross errors over 100 runs)
main_findings: Given identical initializations, k-means# yields lower (better) mean squared error than classical k-means across all datasets tested (Table 1)
Outlier detection using k-means# achieved an overall mean accuracy of 90.4%, precision of 86.8%, recall of 52.4%, and F1-score of 61.1% (Table 2)
Maximum metrics achieved by the algorithm were 99.2% accuracy, 100% precision, 90.0% recall, and 92.9% F1-score
assumptions: K-means, being an instance of the Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), assumes Gaussian data distribution
Nearly all inliers (precisely 99.73%) will have point-to-centroid distances within 3 standard deviations from the population mean
limitations_explicit: Rare cases occur where k-means# returns zero true positives, typically caused by a bad set of randomly selected initial centroids (such as when all initial centroids are outliers), which is a drawback inherited from k-means

potential_open_questions.question: What is the sensitivity of the algorithm to the choice of the number of standard deviations for determining the inlier-outlier distinction threshold?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The choice of 3 standard deviations is fixed in this study, and trade-offs among various performance metrics under varying boundary values remain to be investigated.
potential_open_questions.evidence: It is expected that our choice of 3 standard deviations as the boundary for inlier point-to-centroid distance, plays a role in the performance of the algorithm. We expect trade-offs among the various performance metrics as this value is varied.

potential_open_questions.question: Does the use of cluster-specific thresholds in contrast to a single global threshold improve clustering performance?

parsed_output.paper_title: Adapting k-means Algorithms for Outliers
parsed_output.authors_year: Christoph Grunau and V ́aclav Rozho ́n, 2022
parsed_output.research_question: How to adapt simple and classical sampling-based k-means algorithms to the setting with outliers to obtain stronger theoretical guarantees (outputting (1+e)z outliers and achieving O(1/e)-approximation or O(1)-approximation) while maintaining efficiency?
parsed_output.context: Clustering via the k-means objective is fundamental in machine learning, but sensitive to outliers. The k-means with outliers formulation aims to find k centers and z outliers to minimize the inlier cost. Existing algorithms either require large polynomial time (via linear programming) or output Az outliers for a large constant A, or suffer from at least Omega(z^2) running time.
methods: Reduction from k-means with outliers to k-means with penalties (uniform penalties theta).
Oversampling and sampling-based algorithms inspired by k-means++ and local search (Local-search++).
Metropolis-Hastings algorithm with uniform proposal distribution for sublinear-time sampling speed-ups.
Distributed coordinator model algorithms (generalizing Guha et al. and k-means||).
main_findings: Running oversampled k-means++ with penalties for l = O(k/e) iterations yields an O(1/e)-approximation while outputting (1+e)z outliers.
A sequential sampling-based algorithm (Local-search++ with outliers) achieves an O(1/e)-approximation and outputs (1+e)z outliers in time O~(nk/e).
A distributed algorithm in the coordinator model achieves an O(1)-approximation and outputs (1+e)z outliers, where each machine sends O~(k/e) bits.
An O(1)-approximation algorithm running in time O~(nk^2/z) with O(z) outliers using Metropolis-Hastings sampling, complemented by a matching lower bound of Omega(nk^2/z) in the oracle model.
assumptions: The minimum distance between any two points in X is bounded by 1 and the maximum distance Delta is bounded by poly(n).
Metric spaces and general metric space query models where distances are accessed via an oracle.
limitations_explicit: Algorithms require guessing or trying O(log(nDelta^2)) powers of 2 for the penalty threshold theta since OPT is unknown.
Some improved versions require O(k/e) oversampling of centers or large polynomial running time (e.g., KLS18) in subroutines.

potential_open_questions.question: Can the running time complexity be further reduced to completely eliminate polynomial dependencies on 1/e in terms of exact (1+e)-approximation matching lower bounds?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: Current sampling-based algorithms require oversampling factors like O(k/e) or trade approximation ratios against outlier inflation bounds.
potential_open_questions.evidence: Remark 2 in the paper discusses potential refinements to achieve O~(nk^2/(z 	ext{poly}(e))) with (1+e)-approximation, but leaves it unproven.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: Refining the local search and distributed reductions using almost-metric space transformations can yield an (O(1/poly(e)), 1+e)-approximation algorithm with running time O~(nk^2/(z 	ext{poly}(e))).
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Extending standard metric properties to weighted settings and employing advanced core-sets or multi-round distributed primitives may bypass current additive factor bottlenecks.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: Remark 2 states the authors' belief that refined proofs using Appendices C and F can achieve this bound.

parsed_output.authors_year: Olga Dorabiala, J. Nathan Kutz, Aleksandr Y. Aravkin, 2022
parsed_output.research_question: How can the k-means algorithm be extended to simultaneously cluster points and identify outliers while handling both single- and multi-membership data effectively?
parsed_output.context: Clustering is fundamental in unsupervised learning but is often compromised by a lack of clear separation between groups, noisy observations, and outlying data points. Current robustification methods are specialized for either single-membership or multi-membership data and do not perform competitively in both regimes.
methods: Relaxing the k-means objective to allow point membership to take continuous values in the capped simplex
Developing Robust Trimmed k-means (RTKM) to simultaneously classify points and identify outliers using a novel optimization framework
Using Proximal Alternating Minimization (PAM) updates for the weight matrix and outlier vector, combined with Gauss-Seidel center updates

Evaluating performance on single-membership datasets with outliers (Breast Cancer Wisconsin, shuttle training data) and multi-membership datasets with/without outliers (yeast, scene, emotions) using average F1 score and Me score
Nonparametric statistical validation using the Friedman test and Nemenyi post-hoc test
main_findings: RTKM performs competitively with KMOR on single-membership data containing outliers and with NEO-k-means on multi-membership data without outliers.
On multi-membership data containing outliers, RTKM achieves the highest average F1 scores across all datasets tested and superior outlier detection under alternative noise models.
The Friedman test and Nemenyi post-hoc test show that RTKM significantly outperforms NEO-k-means in outlier identification, while holding the lowest average rank overall.
assumptions: The proportion of expected outliers alpha is specified or estimated beforehand.
The minimum number of clusters s that each point can belong to is known or set by the user.
limitations_explicit: Currently, there is no principled approach to estimating the parameters alpha and s automatically.
NEO-k-means by design cannot identify outliers when k=1 and cannot be restricted to single-membership on data with outliers.

potential_open_questions.question: How can parameters like alpha and s be estimated in a principled manner rather than chosen heuristically?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: There is currently no principled approach to estimating these parameters, requiring users to test a range of values.
potential_open_questions.evidence: Currently, there is no principled approach to estimating these parameters. However, we demonstrate that RTKM performs competitively...

potential_open_questions.question: Can the objective function of RTKM be integrated into adaptive cluster-number estimation algorithms like X-means or G-means?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: Methods such as X-means and G-means estimate k by running k-means repeatedly, but have not yet been adapted to use RTKM's relaxed robust objective function.
potential_open_questions.evidence: Methods such as X-means and G-means have addressed the problem of estimating the number of clusters... Future work could address how these methods could be altered to use our objective function to estimate k.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: Incorporating the RTKM objective function into X-means or G-means frameworks will allow principled, automated estimation of both the number of clusters k and outlier proportions.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Existing cluster-estimation methods rely on standard k-means variants; embedding a robust relaxed formulation should extend clustering structure discovery to noisy multi-membership spaces.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: Methods such as X-means and G-means have addressed the problem of estimating the number of clusters... Future work could address how these methods could be altered to use our objective function to estimate k.

parsed_output.paper_title: Clustering what Matters: Optimal Approximation for Clustering with Outliers
parsed_output.authors_year: Akanksha Agrawal, Tanmay Inamdar, Saket Saurabh, Jie Xue (2023)
parsed_output.research_question: How to design a general approach (FPT reduction) for solving clustering with outliers problems (such as k-MedianOut and k-MeansOut) that matches the approximation ratio of their outlier-free counterparts?
parsed_output.context: Real world data contain noise and outliers that can substantially alter the clusters obtained by standard algorithms. Clustering problems with outliers require excluding m points from a set X of n points and partitioning the remaining points into k clusters to minimize a cost function. Previous algorithms either had suboptimal approximation ratios or required high complexity. This paper studies FPT approximation algorithms parameterized by k, m, and epsilon.
methods: Formulating a lower bound instance of (k + m)-Median (or (k + m, z)-Clustering) with a facility co-located with each client.
Using a polynomial-time tau-approximation algorithm on the lower bound instance to obtain a set of centers A.
Partitioning the points into disjoint sets Xi based on closest centers in A, and further partitioning each Xi into concentric rings Xi,j based on distances to ci.
Constructing a weighted coreset S by sampling points from each ring Xi,j and assigning appropriate integer weights.
Proving concentration bounds and a cost preservation lemma (Lemma 1 and Lemma 2) showing the union of sampled points preserves clustering cost even after excluding m outliers.
Enumerating all subsets T of S of size at most m.
Solving the resulting weighted k-median instances using a beta-approximation algorithm as a black box and selecting the best center set.
main_findings: A general approximation-preserving reduction from k-MedianOut to k-Median running in ((k + m)/epsilon)^{O(m)} * T(n, k) * n^{O(1)} time.
Obtaining a (1 + 2/e + epsilon)-approximation for k-MedianOut and a (1 + 8/e + epsilon)-approximation for k-MeansOut in general metrics.
Achieving (1 + epsilon)-approximations for k-MedianOut and k-MeansOut in metric spaces of constant doubling dimensions, bounded treewidth graphs, and minor-excluded graphs.
Extending the framework to matroid median with outliers, colorful k-median, and general (k, z)-clustering with outliers.
assumptions: Existence of a beta-approximation algorithm for the outlier-free k-Median (or k-Median equivalent) problem.
Existence of a polynomial-time tau-approximation algorithm for the (k + m)-Median instance to obtain initial center sets.
limitations_explicit: The running time has an FPT dependence on the number of outliers m (i.e., ((k + m)/epsilon)^{O(m)}).
The coreset construction requires weights to be integers (addressed by splitting small and large point sets).

potential_open_questions.question: Can the FPT running time dependence on the number of outliers m be removed or improved?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The current enumeration phase over subsets of the coreset of size m leads to an O(m) exponent in the running time bound.
potential_open_questions.evidence: Section 5 explicitly highlights the question of whether an FPT dependence on m is necessary or if approximation guarantees matching outlier-free versions can be achieved in time FPT in k and epsilon alone.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: It is possible to obtain approximation guarantees for k-MedianOut matching those for k-Median with a running time that is FPT in k and epsilon alone, eliminating the dependence on m.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: If more compact coresets or alternative structural properties of outlier locations can be exploited, exhaustive enumeration of size m subsets from the coreset might be bypassed.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: Section 5 poses this as a fundamental open direction for future research.

parsed_output.research_question: How can job placement waiting times and job linearity among female science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) graduates be analyzed and predicted using an integrated clustering and multi-target classification approach?
parsed_output.context: The study addresses workforce gender disparities and the underrepresentation of women in STEM fields by analyzing graduate employment outcomes—specifically job waiting time and job linearity—using institutional records from private universities in Indonesia.
methods: Data pre-processing including null checking, duplicate removal, and outlier detection using the interquartile range (IQR) method
Data augmentation using ADASYN-Gaussian to address class imbalance for female alumni records
K-means least trimmed square (LTS) clustering with hyperparameter tuning for cluster number (k) and trimming percentage
Multi-target random forest (MTRF) classification with Grid search hyperparameter tuning to simultaneously predict job waiting time and job linearity
10-fold cross-validation for model stability and performance evaluation using micro- and macro-averaged F1 scores
main_findings: K-means LTS clustering with k = 2 and a 30% trimming rate achieved a silhouette score of 0.77, outperforming standard K-means (0.63).

Clustering separated female alumni into two distinct groups: Cluster 0 (long waiting time, lower GPA, average study duration 4.13 years) and Cluster 1 (short waiting time, higher GPA, average study duration 4.11 years).
73% of the analyzed female alumni belonged to the short job waiting time group.
The MTRF classification model achieved an overall F1-micro score of 92.2% (0.9221) and an F1-macro score of 90.3% (0.9032).
Confusion matrix evaluation revealed 100% accuracy for the waiting time feature and 81% accuracy for the job linearity feature.
assumptions: Synthetic data generated via ADASYN-Gaussian accurately reflects the underlying multivariate distribution of the minority class.
The selected features from academic and employment records are relevant indicators of graduate employability outcomes.
Female alumni records isolated after data augmentation are sufficient for modeling female STEM graduate outcomes.
limitations_explicit: The features used to predict job linearity may not fully capture real-world factors influencing job relevance, such as job type, industry alignment, or personal career preferences.
The dataset was limited to female graduates from a small sample of private universities, which may affect the generalizability of the findings.

potential_open_questions.evidence: Section 4 suggests applying alternative multi-target learners such as deep neural networks or ensemble methods to improve generalizability for complex targets.

research_gaps.gap: Lack of exact limiting distributions and asymptotic convergence rates for empirical trimmed k-means estimators
research_gaps.why_it_matters: Understanding asymptotic distribution and rates is essential for constructing rigorous statistical hypothesis tests and confidence regions for trimmed cluster centers.
research_gaps.what_is_known: Strong consistency of empirical trimmed k-means and trimmed k-variation has been established under continuity of the limit probability distribution using Skorohod representation and continuity arguments.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: Deriving the exact limiting distribution and convergence rates remains unproven due to discontinuities of the trimming functions on the boundaries of the optimal balls.

evidence.evidence: Section 3 mentions that trimming functions are discontinuous on the boundary of corresponding balls, requiring careful handling of convergences without providing a full central limit theorem for trimmed k-means.

research_gaps.gap: Characterization of universal breakdown points for robust and trimmed k-means under non-spherical or complex cluster structures
research_gaps.why_it_matters: Universal breakdown bounds are critical for guaranteeing the mathematical safety and fault tolerance of clustering models under adversarial or heavy contamination.
research_gaps.what_is_known: Breakdown behaviors have been analyzed for spherical distributions and under specific assumptions where datasets contain balanced clusters covered by balls of bounded radius separated by a minimum distance.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: How breakdown points can be explicitly bounded or improved when clusters have unequal proportions, complex shapes, or overlapping boundaries without strict separation requirements.

evidence.evidence: Section 5 discusses an example where the breakdown point of the alpha-trimmed k-means can be as close to 0 as desired depending on the configuration and data distribution.
The analysis in Section 3.3 and Theorem 2 requires centers of the balls to be at least v apart.

research_gaps.gap: Elimination of polynomial FPT dependencies on the number of outliers in exact approximation reduction frameworks
research_gaps.why_it_matters: Reducing polynomial and parameterized dependencies on outlier size $m$ is vital for establishing tight theoretical lower bounds and scalable complexity guarantees in general metric spaces.
research_gaps.what_is_known: General approximation-preserving reductions and coresets achieve $((k + m)/epsilon)^{O(m)}$ time bounds and polynomial approximations for k-MeansOut and k-MedianOut.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: Whether the FPT dependence on $m$ in the running time bound can be completely removed or improved to match outlier-free versions in time dependent on $k$ and epsilon alone.

evidence.evidence: Section 5 explicitly highlights the question of whether an FPT dependence on m is necessary or if approximation guarantees matching outlier-free versions can be achieved in time FPT in k and epsilon alone.

research_gaps.gap: Adaptive cluster-number estimation integrated into continuous-relaxation and robust trimmed k-means frameworks
research_gaps.why_it_matters: Real-world datasets rarely contain a known number of clusters k or a fixed proportion of outliers alpha. Relying on heuristic trial-and-error or external pre-specification limits the practical autonomy of robust clustering algorithms.
research_gaps.what_is_known: Optimization frameworks like Robust Trimmed k-means (RTKM) effectively handle single- and multi-membership data with outliers via continuous relaxation and proximal alternating minimization, and standalone methods like X-means or G-means address cluster number estimation in standard k-means.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: How RTKM's relaxed robust objective function can be seamlessly coupled with splitting or growth criteria (such as those in X-means or G-means) to simultaneously and adaptively determine both the number of clusters and trimming quotas without manual parameter tuning remains unaddressed.

evidence.evidence: Methods such as X-means and G-means have addressed the problem of estimating the number of clusters... Future work could address how these methods could be altered to use our objective function to estimate k.

research_gaps.gap: Extension of robust outlier-aware k-means update rules to handle non-convex and highly complex high-dimensional manifolds without reliance on linear dimensionality reduction
research_gaps.why_it_matters: Many high-dimensional datasets (such as anomaly and intrusion detection benchmarks) contain non-convex structures or complex manifolds where standard Euclidean distance metrics and linear projection techniques like PCA fail to preserve intrinsic topology.
research_gaps.what_is_known: Modified centroid update frameworks and robust variants (such as K-means# and KM*) successfully mitigate outlier distortion using standard deviation thresholds and iterative point removal, but their geometric mechanics are largely tailored to low-dimensional convex settings.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: How to formulate distance metrics and local thresholding rules for trimmed centroid updates that operate directly on non-convex manifolds or high-dimensional spaces without heavy reliance on preliminary linear dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA.

evidence.evidence: This method inherits the characteristics of the K-means algorithm and has better performance on low-dimensional convex data sets. ODDS data sets are mostly high-dimensional data. In order not to affect the experimental effect, we must reduce the dimensionality...

research_gaps.gap: Replacement of non-robust sample mean and covariance estimators with robust alternatives like minimum-covariance-determinant (MCD) in federated and auto-thresholding k-means architectures
research_gaps.why_it_matters: In distributed or federated outlier-aware clustering frameworks, the initial benign calibration window can be contaminated by edge corruption or initial noise, leading to degraded recall if the underlying covariance model itself is non-robust.
research_gaps.what_is_known: Adaptive auto-thresholding mechanisms (such as Median Absolute Deviation and target-FPR calibration in AF-BKM) successfully improve precision and mitigate merge-induced decay across distributed worker nodes.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: While the thresholding rules themselves are robust, the underlying Gaussian sample mean and covariance estimators used for distance calibration remain vulnerable to dirty commissioning windows, arguing for the integration of robust estimators like MCD.

evidence.evidence: The threshold rule survives contamination; the Gaussian model is the weak point, which argues for MCD or another robust covariance estimator.

research_gaps.why_it_matters: IoT networks span heterogeneous operational environments where devices experience continuous behavioral drift and feature-space skew. research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: How to extend robust anomaly-trimmed federated k-means frameworks to handle streaming concept drift, per-device behavioral drift, and feature-space skew without requiring constant manual anchor recalibration remains unexplored.

evidence.evidence: The non-IID setting primarily models label skew with a small viability floor, lacking deeper treatment of feature-space skew and per-device behavioral drift.

analysis.paper_title: Some Methods for Classification and Analysis of Multivariate Observations
analysis.research_question: How can an N-dimensional population be partitioned into k sets on the basis of a sample to achieve efficient within-class variance, and what is the asymptotic behavior of the k-means process?
analysis.context: The work stems from problems in optimal classification related to optimal information structures and economical data processing on digital computers for similarity grouping, nonlinear prediction, distribution approximation, and independence tests.
methods: Mathematical analysis using martingale theory and measure theory
Computer experiments on multivariate data samples (e.g., student environments, semantic differential measurements, documents, physiological observations)
main_findings: The k-means procedure converges almost surely under specific continuity and boundedness assumptions.
The k-means process can be adapted for similarity grouping, relevant classifications, distribution approximation, and a scrambled dimension test for independence.
assumptions: Probability measure p is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on EN.
p(R) = 1 for a closed and bounded convex set R in EN, with p(A) > 0 for every open set A in R.
limitations_explicit: The k-means procedure will not in general converge to an optimal partition, although there are special cases where it will.

potential_open_questions.question: Can the k-means process be modified or bounded to eliminate slow indefinite oscillations around the center in certain symmetric distributions?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: Theorem 1 establishes almost sure convergence but does not eliminate potential slow oscillations around the center.
potential_open_questions.evidence: The k-means thus converge to some such relative position, but theorem 1 does not quite permit us to eliminate the interesting possibility that the two means oscillate slowly but indefinitely around the center.

potential_open_questions.question: What is the exact statistical power of the proposed scrambled dimension test for independence across various high-dimensional settings?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: Lack of an available computer program to run large numbers of scrambled samples using punched cards during the study.
potential_open_questions.evidence: The power of this procedure remains to be seen. A computer program was not available to do the scrambling, and its being inconvenient to set up large numbers of scrambled samples using punched cards, further testing of this method was not undertaken.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: For fixed marginal distributions, the within-class variance for the optimal partition is maximal when the joint distribution is actually the product of the marginals.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Intuition and inspection of sample behavior suggest that scrambling to destroy relationships increases the within-class variance.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: On the encouraging side is the related conjecture, that for fixed marginal distributions, the within-class variance for the optimal partition as defined in section 1 is maximal when the joint distribution is actually the product of the marginals.

analysis.paper_title: TRIMMED k-MEANS: AN ATTEMPT TO ROBUSTIFY QUANTIZERS
analysis.authors_year: J. A. Cuesta-Albertos, A. Gordaliza and C. Matrán (1997)
analysis.research_question: How can k-means clustering be robustified against outliers using impartial trimming, and what are the existence, characterization, and strong consistency properties of such trimmed k-means?
analysis.context: Traditional k-means clustering and joint location M-estimators can be highly unstable and lack robustness in the presence of outliers or contamination. While trimming procedures are useful, standard techniques suffer from arbitrariness in selecting zones for data removal. Building on Gordaliza's impartial trimming concept, this paper extends trimming to robustify k-means and analyzes its theoretical consistency.
methods: Formulation of impartial trimming functions and trimmed k-variation using penalty functions
Mathematical proofs for the existence and characterization of trimmed k-means
Proof of strong consistency of empirical trimmed k-means using the Skorohod representation theorem and continuity results
Simulation studies on bivariate normal distributions with mixture contamination (outliers and inliers) to evaluate robustness and mean estimation bias
Simulated annealing-based random optimization algorithm implemented in Matlab to handle the nonexistence of deterministic optimal algorithms
main_findings: The optimal trimming function essentially coincides with the indicator function of a nonpathological set formed by the union of k balls of equal radius (Corollary 3.2)
Trimmed k-means induces a partition of the optimal ball into k clusters, and each cluster center is a penalty-mean of X given that cluster (Proposition 3.3)
Proof of existence of trimmed k-means under mild continuity and growth conditions on the penalty function (Theorem 3.1)
Proof of strong consistency of trimmed k-means and trimmed k-variation under continuity of the limit probability distribution (Theorem 3.6)

Simulations show the method successfully detects anomalies and estimates cluster means, though a bias appears at low trimming levels due to probability mass distribution on the boundary of trimming balls
assumptions: The penalty function Phi is continuous, nondecreasing, with Phi(0)=0 and Phi(x) < infinity for all x
The probability measure PX of the limit random vector is continuous
The number of clusters k and the trimming level alpha are given and fixed
limitations_explicit: There is no deterministic optimal algorithm to choose the optimal trimming set, requiring heuristic optimization such as simulated annealing (Sections 1 and 4)

The theoretical breakdown point depends heavily on the data and can be low if the underlying distribution contains dense mass concentrations or contamination proportional to cluster weights (Section 5)
All clusters obtained by the method are forced to be spherical and have the same radius (Corollary 3.2 and Section 4)

potential_open_questions.question: How can the breakdown point of alpha-trimmed k-means be explicitly bounded or improved when clusters have unequal proportions or complex shapes?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The breakdown point depends heavily on the data structure and underlying cluster probabilities rather than being universally robust across all configurations.
potential_open_questions.evidence: Section 5 discusses an example where the breakdown point of the alpha-trimmed k-means can be as close to 0 as desired depending on the configuration and data distribution.

potential_open_questions.question: What are the exact asymptotic convergence rates and limiting distributions for empirical trimmed k-means estimators?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: While strong consistency is established, deriving the exact limiting distribution is complicated by discontinuities of the trimming functions on the boundaries of the balls.
potential_open_questions.evidence: Section 3 mentions that trimming functions are discontinuous on the boundary of corresponding balls, requiring careful handling of convergences without providing a full central limit theorem for trimmed k-means.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: If the penalty function Phi is continuously differentiable and strictly convex, then there is no probability mass at the boundary between clusters.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Smoothness and strict convexity eliminate boundary ambiguity in cluster assignments and partition geometry.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: Section 3 cites previous work (Cuesta-Albertos, Gordaliza and Matrán, 1995) establishing this property under continuously differentiable, strictly convex penalty functions.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: For a probability Q supported by exactly k clusters with respective probabilities q_1, ..., q_k, the breakdown point of the alpha-trimmed k-mean is at most min(alpha, q_1, ..., q_k) independently of the penalty function.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Contamination exceeding the relative mass of individual natural clusters forces the estimator to capture anomalous points as valid clusters or trim valid data.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: Section 5 analyzes the behavior of trimmed k-means under contaminated discrete uniform setups and deduces bounds on the breakdown behavior relative to cluster probabilities.
