parsed_output.authors_year: Hongfu Liu, Junxiang Chen, Jennifer Dy, and Yun Fu, 2023
parsed_output.research_question: How can complex and non-standard cluster analysis problems be unified and solved using generalized K-means frameworks?
parsed_output.context: K-means is a fundamental clustering algorithm widely used due to its simplicity and efficiency, with proven theoretical links to PCA, NMF, and spectral clustering under squared Euclidean distance. However, standard K-means is limited to standard clustering and cannot directly solve complex, non-standard machine learning problems without transformation.
methods: Unifying generalized K-means across four aspects: data input, distance measure, label assignment, and centroid updating.

Formulating data transformations such as kernel methods, one-hot encoding for binary matrices, co-association matrix decomposition, matrix concatenation with auxiliary zeros, and auxiliary binary matrices.
Developing modified distance measures such as point-to-centroid (P2C) distance and Bregman divergences.
Employing non-exhaustive and overlapping label assignments (such as K-means-- and NEO-K-means).
Applying incomplete centroid updating strategies to ignore auxiliary zeros or missing values.
main_findings: Iterative subspace projection and clustering (discriminative clustering) is equivalent to kernel K-means with a specific kernel Gram matrix.
Utility-based consensus clustering and spectral ensemble clustering (SEC) can be solved via weighted K-means on binary or co-association matrices, reducing time complexity from O(n^3) to O(n).

Partition-level constrained clustering and unsupervised domain adaptation (single- and multi-source) can be modeled as K-means problems by concatenating original data with side-information/labels and fill-up zeros, using modified distance and incomplete centroid updating.
Joint clustering with outlier removal (COR) transforms the feature space into partition space and solves the Holoentropy-based objective using K-means--.
assumptions: Centroid updating rules must mathematically match the chosen K-means distance function to guarantee algorithmic convergence.
Auxiliary fill-up zeros introduced during matrix concatenation in constrained clustering and domain adaptation do not contribute to distance calculations or centroid updates.
The target cluster number K is predefined or sampled appropriately for basic partition generation.

research_gaps.gap: Lack of exact limiting distributions and asymptotic convergence rates for empirical trimmed k-means estimators
research_gaps.why_it_matters: Understanding asymptotic distribution and rates is essential for constructing rigorous statistical hypothesis tests and confidence regions for trimmed cluster centers.
research_gaps.what_is_known: Strong consistency of empirical trimmed k-means and trimmed k-variation has been established under continuity of the limit probability distribution using Skorohod representation and continuity arguments.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: Deriving the exact limiting distribution and convergence rates remains unproven due to discontinuities of the trimming functions on the boundaries of the optimal balls.

evidence.evidence: Section 3 mentions that trimming functions are discontinuous on the boundary of corresponding balls, requiring careful handling of convergences without providing a full central limit theorem for trimmed k-means.

research_gaps.gap: Characterization of universal breakdown points for robust and trimmed k-means under non-spherical or complex cluster structures
research_gaps.why_it_matters: Universal breakdown bounds are critical for guaranteeing the mathematical safety and fault tolerance of clustering models under adversarial or heavy contamination.
research_gaps.what_is_known: Breakdown behaviors have been analyzed for spherical distributions and under specific assumptions where datasets contain balanced clusters covered by balls of bounded radius separated by a minimum distance.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: How breakdown points can be explicitly bounded or improved when clusters have unequal proportions, complex shapes, or overlapping boundaries without strict separation requirements.

evidence.evidence: Section 5 discusses an example where the breakdown point of the alpha-trimmed k-means can be as close to 0 as desired depending on the configuration and data distribution.
The analysis in Section 3.3 and Theorem 2 requires centers of the balls to be at least v apart.

research_gaps.gap: Elimination of polynomial FPT dependencies on the number of outliers in exact approximation reduction frameworks
research_gaps.why_it_matters: Reducing polynomial and parameterized dependencies on outlier size $m$ is vital for establishing tight theoretical lower bounds and scalable complexity guarantees in general metric spaces.
research_gaps.what_is_known: General approximation-preserving reductions and coresets achieve $((k + m)/epsilon)^{O(m)}$ time bounds and polynomial approximations for k-MeansOut and k-MedianOut.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: Whether the FPT dependence on $m$ in the running time bound can be completely removed or improved to match outlier-free versions in time dependent on $k$ and epsilon alone.

evidence.evidence: Section 5 explicitly highlights the question of whether an FPT dependence on m is necessary or if approximation guarantees matching outlier-free versions can be achieved in time FPT in k and epsilon alone.

research_gaps.gap: Adaptive cluster-number estimation integrated into continuous-relaxation and robust trimmed k-means frameworks
research_gaps.why_it_matters: Real-world datasets rarely contain a known number of clusters k or a fixed proportion of outliers alpha. Relying on heuristic trial-and-error or external pre-specification limits the practical autonomy of robust clustering algorithms.
research_gaps.what_is_known: Optimization frameworks like Robust Trimmed k-means (RTKM) effectively handle single- and multi-membership data with outliers via continuous relaxation and proximal alternating minimization, and standalone methods like X-means or G-means address cluster number estimation in standard k-means.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: How RTKM's relaxed robust objective function can be seamlessly coupled with splitting or growth criteria (such as those in X-means or G-means) to simultaneously and adaptively determine both the number of clusters and trimming quotas without manual parameter tuning remains unaddressed.

evidence.evidence: Methods such as X-means and G-means have addressed the problem of estimating the number of clusters... Future work could address how these methods could be altered to use our objective function to estimate k.

research_gaps.gap: Extension of robust outlier-aware k-means update rules to handle non-convex and highly complex high-dimensional manifolds without reliance on linear dimensionality reduction
research_gaps.why_it_matters: Many high-dimensional datasets (such as anomaly and intrusion detection benchmarks) contain non-convex structures or complex manifolds where standard Euclidean distance metrics and linear projection techniques like PCA fail to preserve intrinsic topology.
research_gaps.what_is_known: Modified centroid update frameworks and robust variants (such as K-means# and KM*) successfully mitigate outlier distortion using standard deviation thresholds and iterative point removal, but their geometric mechanics are largely tailored to low-dimensional convex settings.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: How to formulate distance metrics and local thresholding rules for trimmed centroid updates that operate directly on non-convex manifolds or high-dimensional spaces without heavy reliance on preliminary linear dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA.

evidence.evidence: This method inherits the characteristics of the K-means algorithm and has better performance on low-dimensional convex data sets. ODDS data sets are mostly high-dimensional data. In order not to affect the experimental effect, we must reduce the dimensionality...

research_gaps.gap: Replacement of non-robust sample mean and covariance estimators with robust alternatives like minimum-covariance-determinant (MCD) in federated and auto-thresholding k-means architectures
research_gaps.why_it_matters: In distributed or federated outlier-aware clustering frameworks, the initial benign calibration window can be contaminated by edge corruption or initial noise, leading to degraded recall if the underlying covariance model itself is non-robust.
research_gaps.what_is_known: Adaptive auto-thresholding mechanisms (such as Median Absolute Deviation and target-FPR calibration in AF-BKM) successfully improve precision and mitigate merge-induced decay across distributed worker nodes.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: While the thresholding rules themselves are robust, the underlying Gaussian sample mean and covariance estimators used for distance calibration remain vulnerable to dirty commissioning windows, arguing for the integration of robust estimators like MCD.

evidence.evidence: The threshold rule survives contamination; the Gaussian model is the weak point, which argues for MCD or another robust covariance estimator.

research_gaps.gap: Management of feature-space skew, behavioral drift, and non-IID conditions in real-world federated IoT intrusion detection deployments
research_gaps.why_it_matters: IoT networks span heterogeneous operational environments where devices experience continuous behavioral drift and feature-space skew. Relying solely on static trusted anchors or label skew assumptions exposes intrusion detection systems to false-positive inflation or missed zero-day attacks over time.
research_gaps.what_is_known: Robust benignly anchored aggregation combined with median absolute deviation (MAD) auto-thresholding can prevent merge-induced precision decay and successfully reduce false-positive rates in federated baseline k-means for benchmark IoT datasets.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: How to extend robust anomaly-trimmed federated k-means frameworks to handle streaming concept drift, per-device behavioral drift, and feature-space skew without requiring constant manual anchor recalibration remains unexplored.

evidence.evidence: The non-IID setting primarily models label skew with a small viability floor, lacking deeper treatment of feature-space skew and per-device behavioral drift.
